awd_titl_txt: SBIR Phase I:  Drug Discovery meets Moore's Law: Synthesizing DNA-Encoded Libraries with Electronics
awd_abstract_narration:
The broader impact of this Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) Phase I project is to accelerate drug discovery. Despite massive investment, the pace of drug development is slow and appears to be slowing further, with new drugs taking an average of 15 years from discovery to market approval. This project aims to develop hardware that will permit the rapid and inexpensive synthesis of DNA-encoded libraries (DELs). This will not only expedite finding drugs for challenging diseases but also generate valuable data for training artificial intelligence (AI) models to improve drug prediction. Commercially, this technology will strengthen U.S. competitiveness in drug discovery and reinforce its leadership in automation and AI research. It could also aid in biodefense, enabling faster responses to emerging biological and chemical threats.	
	 	 	 		
The proposed project straddles three different disciplines – electronics, chemistry, and material science – requiring specialized knowledge and expertise in each. Electronics have come to dominate our world as an information processing technology. Its function is to manipulate voltage values, representing the 1's and 0's encoding data. This project proposes a means of chemical processing with electronics. The goal is to build a device that can perform combinatorial chemistry on nanoliter to picoliter volume droplets, on an electronic substrate. This will be applied to the task of synthesizing DELs. Unlike liquid-handling robots, the technology has no moving or mechanical parts. Instead, it manipulates droplets with electric charge. Software controls the switching of the voltages on a grid of electrodes, dispensing, moving, splitting, merging, and mixing droplets.  The research addresses key technical challenges, including the durability of dielectric and hydrophobic materials, and optimizing electric field control. The chemical protocols for synthesizing DELs will be adapted to novel physical and chemical constraints, including very small volumes. Mitigating contamination is a significant technical risk, requiring innovations in the design, material science, and chemical protocols.

This award reflects NSF's statutory mission and has been deemed worthy of support through evaluation using the Foundation's intellectual merit and broader impacts review criteria.

por.por_cntn:
FemtoFluidics has developed a new type of "bioprocessor" that could transform how scientists discover new medicines. Unlike conventional laboratory robots, the device has no moving or mechanical parts. Instead, it moves tiny droplets of liquid across an electronic grid using electric charge—a principle called electrowetting. Software controls the switching of voltages on thousands of electrodes, enabling droplets to be dispensed, moved, split, merged, and mixed. This approach brings the power of electronics to biology, enabling thousands of experiments to run simultaneously on a single device.

The challenge addressed is significant. Discovering a new drug typically takes years and costs millions of dollars, with most efforts failing. Scientists must synthesize and test countless molecular variants to find ones that work, but existing laboratory equipment cannot keep pace with the number of possibilities that need to be explored.

The FemtoFluidics platform integrates multiple capabilities onto a single device. Heating and cooling elements beneath the grid provide precise temperature control for chemical reactions. Magnetic elements enable washing and purification steps using paramagnetic beads. A sealed, oil-filled environment prevents evaporation and contamination between droplets. An integrated fluorescence microscope provides real-time measurements. Sophisticated software abstracts these operations into high-level workflows, allowing users to design experiments without managing individual electrodes.

During Phase I, the team achieved all technical objectives and demonstrated a complete workflow for biological drug discovery on the platform: DNA assembly was successfully performed in nanoliter-sized droplets, creating functional genetic constructs that worked when introduced into bacteria. Cell-free protein expression was demonstrated, producing proteins directly from DNA templates without living cells—a process critical for rapidly testing protein variants.
Quantitative fluorescence measurements were validated for detecting whether proteins bind to their targets, the key readout for drug screening.
The device operated continuously for days, performing hundreds of thousands of droplet operations without errors. Solutions were developed for key technical challenges, including a patented electronic driving scheme that prevents droplets from sticking to the surface, and specialized coatings that eliminate contamination between experiments.

Two patent applications were filed protecting the core innovations in electronic control and library synthesis.

Through the NSF I-Corps program, the team conducted over 100 interviews with potential customers in pharmaceutical and biotechnology companies. Strong demand was discovered for the technology in biologics drug discovery—the field focused on protein-based medicines like antibodies and enzymes. Three pilot programs are now underway with industry and academic partners exploring applications in DNA manufacturing, therapeutic development, and advanced protein expression systems.

The broader impacts of this work extend beyond drug discovery. The platform uses approximately 1,000 times less reagent than conventional methods, reducing both costs and chemical waste. By accelerating the discovery process, the technology could help bring life-saving medicines to patients faster.

Applications may also extend to agriculture, industrial enzymes, and diagnostics.
Phase I established that the core technology works reliably and addresses a real market need. The major technical risks have been retired and customer demand has been demonstrated. In Phase II, the device will be scaled to over one million electrodes and developed into a commercial product capable of transforming how therapeutic molecules are discovered.
